specs.name: uppercase_word
specs.rule: Lowercase word -> the same word fully uppercased.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize (word->Word): same whole-word case transform, just a different target case; pure copy-with-case is what capitalize already tests.
specs.generation_recipe: Read common_words.txt; keep alphabetic entries, len>=3, all-lowercase. output = word.upper(). Exclude words containing non a-z chars. Dedup. Self-check: assert output.lower()==input.

specs.name: lowercase_word
specs.rule: Fully uppercased word -> the same word fully lowercased.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: lowercase_first_letter (WORD->w): same uppercase-input regime; whole-word lowering is a strictly simpler copy op than letter extraction.
specs.generation_recipe: Read common_words.txt; keep alphabetic len>=3 words. input = word.upper(), output = word (lowercase). Exclude non a-z. Dedup. Self-check: input.lower()==output.

specs.name: first_two_letters
specs.rule: Word -> its first two letters, lowercase.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter ('whose'->'W'): identically start-anchored extraction; two chars at word start usually align with the first BPE token.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=4. output = word[:2]. No case change. Dedup inputs. Self-check: word.startswith(output) and len(output)==2.

specs.name: last_two_letters
specs.rule: Word -> its last two letters, lowercase.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter ('skunk'->'K'): same end-anchored access, extracting two chars instead of one; end-of-word is the second-easiest anchor.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=4. output = word[-2:]. Dedup inputs. Self-check: word.endswith(output) and len(output)==2.

specs.name: first_three_letters
specs.rule: Word -> its first three letters, lowercase.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter: start-anchored prefix extraction; 3-char prefixes often coincide with a whole leading BPE token, keeping it copy-like.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=5 (so the prefix is a proper substring). output = word[:3]. Dedup. Self-check: word.startswith(output) and len(output)==3.

specs.name: remove_first_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the word with its first letter deleted.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter: the op is anchored at the word start, but requires re-emitting the remainder, so one notch harder than pure letter extraction.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 4-8 (short words keep the copied remainder token-simple). output = word[1:]. Dedup. Self-check: input[0]+output==input.

specs.name: remove_last_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the word with its last letter deleted.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter: end-anchored op; output is a copy of the input truncated by one char, harder than extraction but the copy prefix helps ICL.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 4-8. output = word[:-1]. Dedup. Self-check: output+input[-1]==input.

specs.name: prev_capital_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the alphabet predecessor of its first letter, uppercased.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_capital_letter ('hammock'->'I'): exact mirror (predecessor instead of successor of the first letter), same two-step first-letter + alphabet-neighbor op.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words; EXCLUDE words starting with 'a' (no predecessor). output = chr(ord(word[0])-1).upper(). Dedup. Self-check: ord(output.lower())+1==ord(input[0]).

specs.name: next_letter_of_last_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the alphabet successor of its LAST letter, uppercased.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_capital_letter: same alphabet-successor op moved to the last letter; combines the working capitalize_last_letter access pattern with the working successor op.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words; EXCLUDE words ending in 'z'. output = chr(ord(word[-1])+1).upper(). Dedup. Self-check: ord(output.lower())-1==ord(input[-1]).

specs.name: starts_with_vowel
specs.rule: Word -> 'vowel' if its first letter is one of a,e,i,o,u, else 'consonant'.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter + sentiment: first-letter access (easy anchor) followed by a 2-way label, like sentiment's binary output format.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=3. 'y' counts as consonant (state this in task doc). output = 'vowel' if word[0] in 'aeiou' else 'consonant'. Sample to roughly 50/50 class balance (vowel-initial words are ~20% of the list; the list still has >2000 of them). Dedup.

specs.name: ends_with_vowel
specs.rule: Word -> 'vowel' if its last letter is one of a,e,i,o,u, else 'consonant'.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter + sentiment: last-letter access with a binary label; end anchor is proven workable by capitalize_last_letter.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=3; EXCLUDE words ending in 'y' (ambiguous vowel status). output = 'vowel' if word[-1] in 'aeiou' else 'consonant'. Sample to ~50/50 balance. Dedup.

specs.name: contains_letter_e
specs.rule: Word -> 'yes' if the letter e occurs anywhere in it, else 'no'.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: count_vowels: whole-word letter scanning, but reduced to a binary presence query, which is easier than exact counting.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 3-9. output = 'yes' if 'e' in word else 'no'. Sample to 50/50 balance (e is common: bias sampling toward no-class words, still >3000 available). Dedup.

specs.name: ends_with_ing
specs.rule: Word -> 'yes' if it ends with the letters 'ing', else 'no'.
specs.domain_source: gerunds of common_verbs.txt via lemminflect + non-ing words from common_nouns.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: suffix-sensitive word classification; '-ing' is a single highly salient BPE suffix token, so detection is near-trivial for GPT-J.
specs.generation_recipe: yes-class: for each verb in common_verbs.txt take lemminflect getInflection(verb,'VBG'); keep only outputs actually ending 'ing' (~3500). no-class: common_nouns.txt entries NOT ending 'ing'. Balance 50/50, dedup across classes. Self-check: label == word.endswith('ing').

specs.name: alphabet_position_first_letter
specs.rule: Word (first letter restricted to a-j) -> the alphabet position (1-10) of its first letter.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt filtered to first letter in a-j
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_capital_letter: same first-letter access composed with alphabet knowledge; restricting to positions 1-10 keeps the ordinal lookup in the well-known early-alphabet range.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, keep words whose word[0] is in 'abcdefghij'. output = str(ord(word[0])-96). Stratify so each of the 10 first letters appears; dedup. Self-check: 1<=int(output)<=10 and chr(96+int(output))==input[0].

specs.name: first_vowel
specs.rule: Word -> the first vowel (a,e,i,o,u) reading left to right.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: count_vowels: same vowel-detection skill, but extraction of the first hit instead of a full count; first vowel sits at position 1-3 in most English words, near the easy word start.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=3; EXCLUDE words with no a/e/i/o/u (e.g. 'myth', 'gym'). output = next(c for c in word if c in 'aeiou'). Dedup. Self-check: output in 'aeiou' and everything before its first occurrence is non-vowel.

specs.name: nato_first_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the NATO phonetic-alphabet codeword for its first letter (e.g. c -> Charlie).
specs.domain_source: common_words.txt + hardcoded 24-entry NATO table (letters a and j excluded)
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_capital_letter: first-letter access composed with a single very common lookup table; the NATO alphabet is heavily represented in pretraining data.
specs.generation_recipe: Hardcode the standard NATO table {b:Bravo, c:Charlie, ..., z:Zulu}; EXCLUDE first letters 'a' (Alfa/Alpha spelling variants) and 'j' (Juliett/Juliet variants) so every answer has one canonical spelling. Domain: common_words.txt words not starting a/j. output = table[word[0]]. Self-check: output[0].lower()==input[0]; scoring should be exact-match on the table spelling.

specs.name: double_last_letter
specs.rule: Word -> the word with its final letter written twice.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: remove_last_letter / singular-plural: copy the word then modify the end, like plural's copy+suffix but purely orthographic; non-word outputs make it harder, hence medium.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 3-6; EXCLUDE words already ending in a doubled letter (e.g. 'ball', 'free') so the pattern is visually unambiguous in prompts. output = word + word[-1]. Dedup. Self-check: output[:-1]==input and output[-1]==input[-1].

specs.name: third_letter
specs.rule: Word -> its third letter, lowercase.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_second_letter ('chinchilla'->'H'): one position deeper and no case flip; deepest still-plausible positional extraction for GPT-J.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len>=4. output = word[2] (no case change, distinguishing it from the capitalize_* family). Dedup. Self-check: input[2]==output.

specs.name: titlecase_phrase
specs.rule: Two-word lowercase phrase -> the phrase with each word capitalized.
specs.domain_source: common_adjs.txt x common_nouns.txt bigrams
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize (word->Word): the identical case transform applied per word of a bigram; title-casing phrases is ubiquitous in pretraining (headlines, titles).
specs.generation_recipe: Sample adj from common_adjs.txt (top 1500, alphabetic, len 3-8) and noun from common_nouns.txt (top 2000, same filter); input = f'{adj} {noun}', output = input.title(). Sample ~20000 unique combos, dedup. Self-check: output.lower()==input and both words start uppercase.

specs.name: initials_two_words
specs.rule: Two-word phrase -> the two initials, uppercased and concatenated.
specs.domain_source: common_adjs.txt x common_nouns.txt bigrams
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter applied twice: acronym/initialism formation is a extremely common pattern in pretraining text, and both letters sit at easy word-start anchors.
specs.generation_recipe: Same bigram sampler as titlecase_phrase. output = (adj[0]+noun[0]).upper(). Dedup on input. Self-check: len(output)==2 and output[0].lower()==adj[0] and output[1].lower()==noun[0].

specs.name: first_letter_second_word
specs.rule: Two-word phrase -> the first letter of the SECOND word, lowercase.
specs.domain_source: common_adjs.txt x common_nouns.txt bigrams
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter: same first-letter extraction, retargeted to the second word; word boundaries are token boundaries so the anchor stays easy.
specs.generation_recipe: Same bigram sampler. output = noun[0] (lowercase). Dedup on input; stratify so >=15 distinct output letters occur. Self-check: input.split()[1].startswith(output).

specs.name: count_words
specs.rule: Phrase of 1-4 space-separated words -> the number of words.
specs.domain_source: combinations from common_adjs.txt and common_nouns.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: word_length ('along'->'5'): counting of surface units, but the units are whitespace-separated tokens, which is easier than character counting.
specs.generation_recipe: Build phrases: 1 word = noun; 2 = adj noun; 3 = adj adj noun; 4 = adj adj adj noun, with adjs/nouns drawn from the resource lists (distinct adjs within a phrase). Uniform over lengths 1-4, dedup inputs. output = str(len(input.split())). Self-check trivial.

specs.name: case_of_word
specs.rule: Word shown either ALL-CAPS or all-lowercase -> the label 'upper' or 'lower'.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt, each word in both cases
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment: binary surface classification; case is directly encoded in BPE token identity, so detection (unlike transformation) is essentially free.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic len>=3. For each sampled word pick one form: (word.upper(),'upper') or (word,'lower'), 50/50. A word may appear in at most one case form to keep inputs unique. Dedup. Self-check: input.isupper() == (output=='upper').

specs.name: double_word
specs.rule: Word -> the word written twice, space-separated.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: identity (x->x): pure copying, which transformers do perfectly, plus a fixed repeat-twice template; distinct mapping from identity (output != input).
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 3-7 (keeps output <=3 tokens typically). output = f'{word} {word}'. Dedup. Self-check: output.split()==[input,input].

specs.name: count_letter_e
specs.rule: Word -> how many times the letter e occurs in it (0-3).
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: count_vowels: identical counting skill but over a single target letter and including a 0 class; genuinely different count target from vowels/consonants/length.
specs.generation_recipe: common_words.txt, alphabetic words len 3-9; keep only words with word.count('e') <= 3. output = str(word.count('e')). Stratify sampling so counts 0,1,2,3 all appear substantially (0 and 1 dominate naturally; cap them). Dedup. Self-check by rule.

specs.name: first_digit
specs.rule: Given a positive integer written in digits, output its first (leftmost) digit.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 2-6 digits, no leading zeros
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter — same positional-extraction operation, applied to digits instead of letters, no case transform needed so strictly easier
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique random integers uniformly over lengths 2-6 (range 10..999999), seed fixed, dedupe. Output = str(n)[0]. No edge cases: leading zeros impossible for integers. Verify programmatically that output == input[0].

specs.name: last_digit
specs.rule: Given a positive integer written in digits, output its last (rightmost) digit.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 2-6 digits
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter — same last-position extraction on a short symbol string, without the case step
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique random integers over 10..999999, seed fixed, dedupe. Output = str(n)[-1]. Include some inputs ending in 0 deliberately. Verify output == input[-1].

specs.name: second_digit
specs.rule: Given a positive integer with at least two digits, output its second digit from the left.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 2-6 digits
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_second_letter — identical second-position indexing, on digits
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique random integers over 10..999999, seed fixed, dedupe. Output = str(n)[1]. No exclusions needed (all inputs have >= 2 digits). Verify output == input[1].

specs.name: count_digits
specs.rule: Given a positive integer written in digits, output how many digits it has.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 1-6 digits, balanced across lengths
specs.difficulty_anchor: word_length — same length-counting operation on a shorter symbol alphabet; distinct from existing 'magnitude' task, which maps number->number rather than to a count
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers stratified by length: equal counts of 1,2,3,4,5,6-digit numbers (1-digit gives only 9, backfill from other lengths), seed fixed. Output = str(len(str(n))). Verify programmatically.

specs.name: count_zeros
specs.rule: Given a digit string, output how many of its digits are '0'.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 3-6 digits, stratified so zero-counts 0-4 are all represented
specs.difficulty_anchor: count_vowels — counting occurrences of a target symbol class in a short string; here the target class is a single symbol, which is easier
specs.generation_recipe: Generate random integers of length 3-6 (no leading zero); rejection-sample to balance the zero-count label distribution over {0,1,2,3,4} (natural sampling makes high counts rare). Output = str(str(n).count('0')). Verify by recount.

specs.name: largest_digit
specs.rule: Given a positive integer written in digits, output its largest digit.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: random integers with 2-5 digits, all digits distinct
specs.difficulty_anchor: count_consonants — requires scanning all symbols of a short string and aggregating; harder than positional extraction, comparable to counting tasks
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers of length 2-5; require all digits distinct (guarantees a unique argmax and avoids ties confusing evaluation, though ties would not change the answer). Output = max(str(n)). Fixed seed, dedupe, verify by recomputation.

specs.name: round_down_to_hundred
specs.rule: Given an integer >= 101 that is not a multiple of 100, output it rounded down to the nearest multiple of 100.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 101-99999 excluding multiples of 100
specs.difficulty_anchor: lowercase_last_letter — mechanically it is 'replace the last two digits with 00', a positional overwrite akin to positional case ops, and rounding to hundreds is a very common text pattern
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 101..99999 with n % 100 != 0 (multiples of 100 map to themselves, overlapping identity). Output = str((n // 100) * 100). Fixed seed, dedupe, verify arithmetically.

specs.name: round_up_to_ten
specs.rule: Given an integer that is not a multiple of 10, output it rounded up to the next multiple of 10.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 11-9999 excluding multiples of 10
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits — increment the tens 'slot' and zero the units; one small local arithmetic step
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 11..9999 with n % 10 != 0 (multiples of 10 are ambiguous between 'stay' and 'next'). Output = str(((n // 10) + 1) * 10). Fixed seed, dedupe, verify arithmetically. Note this differs from round_down_to_hundred in both direction and granularity.

specs.name: parity_even_odd
specs.rule: Given an integer, output 'even' if it is even and 'odd' if it is odd.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 1-99999, balanced 50/50 by parity
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — binary classification with common-word labels; the decision reduces to the last digit, comparable to last-letter tasks
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 1..99999, stratified to exactly 50% even / 50% odd so label priors are uninformative. Output = 'even' if n % 2 == 0 else 'odd'. Fixed seed, verify programmatically.

specs.name: ordinal_suffix
specs.rule: Given an integer in digits, output the same integer with its English ordinal suffix attached (21 -> 21st, 112 -> 112th).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 1-9999
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past — a single-step, highly conventionalized English formatting transform GPT-J has seen constantly in pretraining
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers 1..9999. Suffix rule: if n % 100 in {11,12,13} -> 'th'; elif n % 10 == 1 -> 'st'; elif n % 10 == 2 -> 'nd'; elif n % 10 == 3 -> 'rd'; else 'th'. Output = str(n) + suffix. Oversample the st/nd/rd cases so 'th' is not >80% of labels. Verify with the same function; unit-test 11,12,13,111,121.

specs.name: double_no_carry
specs.rule: Given an integer all of whose digits are 4 or less, output its double.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers with 2-5 digits, every digit in {0,1,2,3,4}
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits — doubling with all digits <= 4 involves no carries, so it decomposes into independent per-digit doublings, each a trivial single-digit fact
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate integers whose decimal digits are all in {0,1,2,3,4}, lengths 2-5, leading digit in {1,2,3,4}: 4*5 + 4*25 + 4*125 + 4*625 = 3120 items. Output = str(2*n). The digit constraint guarantees carry-free doubling. Verify 2*n and that no digit of n exceeds 4.

specs.name: plus_ten
specs.rule: Given an integer whose tens digit is not 9, output that integer plus 10.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 10-99999 with tens digit != 9
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits — identical increment operation, applied one decimal place higher; carry-free by construction
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 10..99999 with (n // 10) % 10 != 9 (excludes carries into the hundreds, keeping the transform a single-digit edit). Output = str(n + 10). Fixed seed, dedupe, verify arithmetically.

specs.name: minus_ten
specs.rule: Given an integer >= 20 whose tens digit is not 0, output that integer minus 10.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 20-99999 with tens digit != 0
specs.difficulty_anchor: prev_number_digits — same decrement operation one decimal place higher; borrow-free by construction
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 20..99999 with (n // 10) % 10 != 0 (excludes borrows from the hundreds). Output = str(n - 10). Fixed seed, dedupe, verify arithmetically.

specs.name: plus_hundred
specs.rule: Given an integer whose hundreds digit is not 9, output that integer plus 100.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 1-99999 with hundreds digit != 9
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits / plus_ten — single-digit edit at the hundreds place, carry-free by construction
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique integers in 1..99999 with (n // 100) % 10 != 9. Output = str(n + 100). Include some 1-2 digit inputs (47 -> 147) since GPT-J handles prepending '1' well. Fixed seed, dedupe, verify arithmetically.

specs.name: larger_of_pair
specs.rule: Given two distinct integers separated by a space, output the larger one.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: ordered pairs of distinct integers from 1-999
specs.difficulty_anchor: magnitude / identity — output copies one of the two visible inputs; magnitude comparison of small numbers is a robust pretraining skill, and the copy operation matches identity
specs.generation_recipe: Sample pairs (a, b) uniform in 1..999 with a != b; format input as f'{a} {b}'; randomize whether the larger number is first or second (50/50) so position is uninformative. Output = str(max(a, b)). Prefer pairs with different digit counts for ~half the data (easy) and same digit count for the rest. Dedupe on the input string, fixed seed, verify with max().

specs.name: smaller_of_pair
specs.rule: Given two distinct integers separated by a space, output the smaller one.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: ordered pairs of distinct integers from 1-999
specs.difficulty_anchor: larger_of_pair — identical comparison with the opposite selection; useful as a minimal-pair contrast for function-vector geometry
specs.generation_recipe: Same generator as larger_of_pair (independent seed, dedupe against nothing external): pairs (a, b) in 1..999, a != b, position of the smaller randomized 50/50. Output = str(min(a, b)). Verify with min().

specs.name: percent_to_decimal
specs.rule: Given a percentage 'N%' where N is an integer not divisible by 10, output N/100 as a decimal.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 1-9999 excluding multiples of 10, formatted 'N%'
specs.difficulty_anchor: singular-plural — a conventional single-step surface transform (shift the decimal point two places) heavily attested in pretraining text
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique N in 1..9999 with N % 10 != 0 (multiples of 10 create trailing-zero ambiguity: 80% could be 0.8 or 0.80). Input = f'{N}%'; output = f'{N/100:.2f}' i.e. always exactly two decimals ('0.07', '2.63', '12.04'). Weight sampling toward N < 100 (the familiar case) at ~70%. Verify float(output) * 100 == N.

specs.name: iso_date_to_month
specs.rule: Given a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, output the English name of its month.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: valid dates, years 1900-2099, all 12 months, days 1-28
specs.difficulty_anchor: country-capital — a fixed 12-entry lookup (month number -> name) that GPT-J knows cold, wrapped in a field-extraction step; the full-date input keeps the domain far above 1200 despite only 12 labels
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique (year, month, day) with year in 1900..2099, month 1..12 balanced, day 1..28 (always valid, sidesteps month lengths and leap years). Format f'{y:04d}-{m:02d}-{d:02d}'. Output = calendar month name via a hardcoded 12-entry table. Verify with datetime.strptime(...).strftime('%B').

specs.name: iso_date_day_of_month
specs.rule: Given a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, output the day of the month as a plain number (no leading zero).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: valid dates, years 1900-2099, days 1-28 plus 29/30 for long months
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter — positional field extraction with a trivial normalization (strip leading zero), analogous difficulty to single-letter extraction tasks
specs.generation_recipe: Same date generator as iso_date_to_month (independent samples). Output = str(int(dd)), i.e. '03' -> '3'. Ensure roughly uniform coverage of days 1-9 vs 10-28 so the leading-zero-strip rule is demonstrated in every 10-shot prompt (include at least one day < 10 among sampled shots by stratification). Verify int(output) == day.

specs.name: iso_date_year_plus_one
specs.rule: Given a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, output the year one greater than the date's year.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: valid dates, years 1800-2099
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits — extraction of the year field followed by the same +1 increment GPT-J already handles; years are among the most-incremented numbers in pretraining text
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique valid dates with year in 1800..2099, month 1..12, day 1..28. Output = str(year + 1). Keep century-boundary cases (1899 -> 1900, 1999 -> 2000) to at most ~2% of data since they involve carries. Verify arithmetically.

specs.name: day_after_textual_date
specs.rule: Given a date like 'March 5, 1984' with day 1-27, output the month and next day: 'March 6'.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 12 months x days 1-27 x years 1900-2099
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits plus a copy — the month is copied verbatim and the day gets +1; capping days at 27 removes all month-boundary logic
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique (month_name, day, year) with day in 1..27 (never crosses a month boundary, so no month-length or leap-year knowledge is needed) and year in 1900..2099. Input f'{month} {day}, {year}'; output f'{month} {day+1}' (year deliberately dropped from the output to keep it 2 tokens). Verify by parsing and adding timedelta(days=1).

specs.name: year_to_decade
specs.rule: Given a four-digit year, output its decade in the standard 'YYY0s' form (1987 -> 1980s).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: years 1000-2999, excluding years ending in 0
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past — a heavily conventionalized surface transform ('in 1987' -> 'the 1980s') that GPT-J has seen constantly; mechanically it zeroes the last digit and appends 's'
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate years 1000..2999 with last digit != 0 (years like 1980 map to themselves + 's', which is fine, but excluding them keeps the transform visibly non-trivial in every shot): 1800 items. Output = str(y // 10 * 10) + 's'. Weight sampling toward 1500-2099 where decade phrasing is most attested. Verify with the formula.

specs.name: hour_after_time
specs.rule: Given a 24-hour clock time HH:MM with hour 00-22, output the time one hour later (minutes unchanged).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 23 hours x 60 minutes = 1380 distinct times
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits plus a copy — +1 on the hour field with the minutes copied verbatim; excluding hour 23 removes the wraparound case
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate all times f'{h:02d}:{m:02d}' for h in 0..22, m in 0..59 (1380 items, meets the 1200 floor; extend with seconds HH:MM:SS if more are ever needed). Output = f'{h+1:02d}:{m:02d}'. Hour 23 excluded (00:xx wraparound). Note output keeps two-digit zero-padded hours ('09:15'), demonstrated in shots. Verify with the formula.

specs.name: time_extract_minutes
specs.rule: Given a 24-hour clock time HH:MM with minutes 10-59, output the minutes as a number.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 24 hours x minutes 10-59 = 1200 distinct times
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter — pure positional field extraction from a rigid short format
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate f'{h:02d}:{m:02d}' for h in 0..23, m in 10..59 (exactly 1200 items; minutes 00-09 excluded so the answer never needs a leading-zero-strip decision like '04' vs '4'). Output = str(m). Verify output == input.split(':')[1].

specs.name: date_to_quarter
specs.rule: Given a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, output its calendar quarter as Q1, Q2, Q3, or Q4.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: valid dates, years 1900-2099, months balanced across quarters
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news — 4-way classification with fixed short labels; the month->quarter mapping (Jan-Mar=Q1, ...) is a standard business convention in pretraining text
specs.generation_recipe: Sample unique valid dates (year 1900..2099, month 1..12 balanced, day 1..28). Output = 'Q' + str((month - 1) // 3 + 1). Calendar quarters only (explicitly not fiscal-year quarters — state this in any task doc). Verify with the formula; balance labels 25/25/25/25.

specs.name: next_month_of_date
specs.rule: Given 'MonthName Year', output the name of the following month (December -> January).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 12 months x years 1800-2099 = 3600 inputs
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_item — successor in a memorized cyclic sequence, exactly the operation next_item tests on number words, here on month names (the year makes the input domain large; bare month names alone would be a banned 12-item domain)
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate (month, year) for all 12 months x years 1800..2099. Input f'{month_name} {year}'; output = next month name from a hardcoded cyclic list, December -> 'January' (output contains no year, so the wraparound needs no year+1 logic). Verify against calendar.month_name indexing mod 12.

specs.name: prev_month_of_date
specs.rule: Given 'MonthName Year', output the name of the preceding month (January -> December).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 12 months x years 1800-2099 = 3600 inputs
specs.difficulty_anchor: prev_item — predecessor in a memorized cyclic sequence; predecessor tasks run slightly harder than successor tasks, matching the prev_item vs next_item gap
specs.generation_recipe: Same generator as next_month_of_date. Output = previous month name from the hardcoded cyclic list, January -> 'December'. Verify against calendar.month_name indexing mod 12.

specs.name: days_in_month
specs.rule: Given 'MonthName Year' where the month is not February, output the number of days in that month (30 or 31).
specs.domain_source: pure rule: 11 non-February months x years 1800-2099 = 3300 inputs
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — effectively binary classification (30 vs 31) driven by a memorized rhyme-level fact ('Thirty days hath September...'); February is excluded so leap years never matter
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate (month, year) for the 11 months excluding February, years 1800..2099. Output from the fixed table: {Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov} -> '30', {Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec} -> '31'. Balance labels by oversampling 30-day months to ~45%. February is excluded because its length depends on the year (leap rule), which would either break determinism or demand a harder rule. Verify with calendar.monthrange.

specs.name: english-italian
specs.rule: Translate a common English word into its most common single-word Italian equivalent.
specs.domain_source: dataset_files/extended_tasks/_resources/common_words.txt (top 12000 frequency-sorted English words), content words only
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-french / english-spanish — identical task shape, Italian is a comparably high-resource Romance language in web corpora
specs.generation_recipe: Take common_words.txt, drop function words (keep nouns/verbs/adjectives per wordfreq/lemminflect POS). In chunks of 100, have the LLM produce the single dominant Italian translation. EXCLUDE: words with multiple equally common Italian translations, English words whose Italian form is identical (e.g. 'pizza'), and multi-word translations. Self-check: independent second pass translates each Italian word back to English; keep a pair only if round-trip returns the original word (or its lemma); drop all mismatches. Target >=1500 survivors from ~3000 candidates.

specs.name: english-portuguese
specs.rule: Translate a common English word into its most common single-word Portuguese equivalent.
specs.domain_source: common_words.txt (12000 frequency-sorted English words), content words only
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-spanish — Portuguese is very close to Spanish in structure and reasonably represented in the Pile
specs.generation_recipe: Same pipeline as english-italian: filter common_words.txt to content words, translate in chunks of 100 to European/Brazilian-neutral Portuguese, one dominant single-word translation per input. EXCLUDE ambiguous translations, identical spellings, and words whose PT/BR forms differ. Self-check: round-trip back-translation in an independent pass; drop any pair that does not round-trip. Keep diacritics in outputs.

specs.name: english-dutch
specs.rule: Translate a common English word into its most common single-word Dutch equivalent.
specs.domain_source: common_words.txt (12000 frequency-sorted English words), content words only
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-german — Dutch is closely related to German; slightly lower resource so medium confidence
specs.generation_recipe: Same pipeline as english-italian on common_words.txt content words. EXCLUDE: Dutch translations identical to the English word (frequent for Germanic cognates like 'water'->'water'), ambiguous translations, multi-word outputs. Self-check: round-trip back-translation in a separate pass; drop mismatches. Expect a higher exclusion rate than Romance languages; start from ~4000 candidates to net >=1500.

specs.name: french-english
specs.rule: Translate a common French word into its most common single-word English equivalent.
specs.domain_source: French sides of the pairs produced for the existing english-french task pipeline, or common_words.txt translated to French then reversed
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-french — same lexical knowledge, reversed direction; into-English is typically easier for an English-centric model
specs.generation_recipe: Generate EN->FR pairs from common_words.txt content words (chunks of 100), then invert. EXCLUDE: French words with multiple common English senses (e.g. 'livre' = book/pound, 'temps' = time/weather), French-English identical spellings, and any French word appearing as translation of two different English words. Self-check: independent pass translates each French word to English without seeing the intended answer; keep only exact matches (lemma-level).

specs.name: spanish-english
specs.rule: Translate a common Spanish word into its most common single-word English equivalent.
specs.domain_source: Spanish sides of EN->ES pairs generated from common_words.txt, inverted
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-spanish reversed; Spanish is the highest-resource non-English language for GPT-J
specs.generation_recipe: Same invert-the-pipeline recipe as french-english, using Spanish. EXCLUDE polysemous Spanish words (e.g. 'tiempo' = time/weather, 'banco' = bank/bench), ES-EN identical spellings ('hospital', 'animal'), and Spanish words mapped from two English sources. Self-check: blind back-translation pass ES->EN, keep exact lemma matches only.

specs.name: german-english
specs.rule: Translate a common German word into its most common single-word English equivalent.
specs.domain_source: German sides of EN->DE pairs generated from common_words.txt, inverted; German nouns capitalized per orthography
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-german reversed — same lexical knowledge, easier direction
specs.generation_recipe: Invert the EN->DE pipeline over common_words.txt content words. Keep standard German orthography (nouns capitalized). EXCLUDE: DE-EN identical or near-identical cognates ('Hand', 'Winter'), polysemous German words, compounds longer than one word. Self-check: blind back-translation pass DE->EN in a separate context; keep exact matches only.

specs.name: language_identification
specs.rule: Given a common word from French, Spanish, German, or Italian, output the name of the language it belongs to.
specs.domain_source: The verified foreign-word sides of the four translation pipelines above (400+ words per language)
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news — fixed 4-way label set; language ID from orthography is a strong surface cue GPT-J picks up easily
specs.generation_recipe: Pool the verified foreign words from the en->fr/es/de/it pipelines (~600+ each). EXCLUDE: words spelled identically in two or more of the four languages (e.g. 'animale' is IT-only, fine; 'central' appears in FR and ES — drop), words identical to an English word, and proper nouns. Self-check: for each retained word, an independent pass must assert 'this word exists in language L and not in the other three'; drop failures. Balance to ~400 per language.

specs.name: french_noun_gender
specs.rule: Given a common French noun, output its grammatical gender: masculine or feminine.
specs.domain_source: 1500+ common French nouns generated in frequency order by the LLM (seeded from translations of common_nouns.txt)
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-french — same tier of French lexical knowledge; gender is heavily cued by word endings which a 6B model has absorbed
specs.generation_recipe: Translate common_nouns.txt to French (single-word translations only), keep the French nouns. EXCLUDE: nouns usable in both genders ('élève', 'artiste', profession nouns with both forms), nouns whose gender varies by sense ('livre', 'tour' — wait, 'livre' is masculine=book / feminine=pound: DROP such dual-gender words explicitly), plural-only nouns. Self-check: independent pass asks for the article (le/la) for each noun; keep only nouns where article and labeled gender agree and the pass marks it unambiguous.

specs.name: german_noun_gender
specs.rule: Given a common German noun, output its definite article: der, die, or das.
specs.domain_source: 1500+ common German nouns from single-word translations of common_nouns.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-german — same lexical tier; der/die/das completion is an extremely frequent pattern in German web text
specs.generation_recipe: Translate common_nouns.txt to German, keep single-word nouns with standard capitalization. EXCLUDE: nouns with regionally or semantically varying gender ('Joghurt', 'Teil' der/das by sense), plural-only nouns ('Eltern'), and long compounds (>12 characters, to keep tokenization friendly). Output is exactly one of {der, die, das} (all single tokens). Self-check: independent pass produces the article blind; keep only agreements flagged unambiguous.

specs.name: spanish_noun_gender
specs.rule: Given a common Spanish noun, output its grammatical gender: masculine or feminine.
specs.domain_source: 1500+ common Spanish nouns from single-word translations of common_nouns.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: english-spanish — Spanish gender is strongly cued by -o/-a endings, which makes the ICL rule especially learnable
specs.generation_recipe: Translate common_nouns.txt to Spanish, keep single-word nouns. EXCLUDE: common-gender nouns ('estudiante', 'artista'), sense-dependent gender ('capital', 'orden', 'frente'), plural-only nouns. Keep a mix of regular (-o/-a) and irregular endings ('flor', 'mano', 'día') so the mapping is knowledge, not pure orthography, but do not exclude regulars. Self-check: independent el/la article pass; keep only unambiguous agreements.

specs.name: city-country
specs.rule: Given a well-known world city, output the country it is in.
specs.domain_source: Enumerable world knowledge: cities with population >~200k plus historically/touristically famous smaller cities; thousands exist and several thousand are reliably known to LLMs
specs.difficulty_anchor: landmark-country — same relation type (place -> country) with a much larger domain of comparably famous places
specs.generation_recipe: Generate country-by-country: for each of ~120 countries, list 5-40 of its most famous cities (more for large countries), giving ~2500 candidates. EXCLUDE: city names shared across countries unless one referent is overwhelmingly dominant ('Paris' OK -> France; 'San Jose', 'Cordoba', 'Tripoli' DROP), cities renamed recently, and disputed territories. Use everyday country names ('United States', 'South Korea'). Self-check: independent pass answers 'Which country is <city> in?' blind, plus a spot rule that the city has population >200k OR is famous (capital, tourist, historic); drop disagreements and uncertain items.

specs.name: city-continent
specs.rule: Given a well-known world city, output its continent (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, or Australia).
specs.domain_source: Same verified city list as city-country; continent derived deterministically from the verified country via a fixed country->continent table
specs.difficulty_anchor: landmark-country / country-capital — coarser than city-country, but the label must be inferred rather than recalled verbatim, so medium
specs.generation_recipe: Reuse the verified city->country pairs from city-country, then map country->continent with a hardcoded 195-row lookup table (deterministic, no LLM). Label set fixed to {Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Australia}. EXCLUDE: transcontinental-country cities where continent is contested (Istanbul, all Russian cities east of the Urals, Cairo OK as Africa but drop Suez-area edge cases), and Pacific island cities (Oceania-vs-Australia label confusion). Self-check inherited from city-country verification; additionally assert every retained country appears in the lookup table.

specs.name: us-city-state
specs.rule: Given a well-known US city, output the US state it is in.
specs.domain_source: Enumerable knowledge: ~25-35 well-known cities per state across 50 states (state capitals, metro areas, college towns, tourist towns), heavily represented in US-centric web text
specs.difficulty_anchor: national_parks (place -> US state) — identical output space and relation type, larger input domain
specs.generation_recipe: Generate state-by-state: for each of the 50 states list 20-35 well-known cities/towns (capitals, biggest cities, university towns, famous resorts), ~1500 candidates. EXCLUDE: any city name existing in more than one state without a single overwhelmingly dominant referent (DROP Springfield, Portland, Columbus, Aurora, Arlington; KEEP e.g. Boston, Milwaukee where dominance is total — apply a strict 'would a US reader ever need the state to disambiguate?' test and drop if yes). Self-check: independent blind pass 'Which state is <city> in?'; drop disagreements; also verify each retained name is unique in the final list.

specs.name: living_nonliving
specs.rule: Classify a concrete noun as living (organism: animal, plant, or person) or nonliving.
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), filtered by LLM to unambiguous cases
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — binary label from a fixed pair; animacy is one of the most salient semantic features in embedding space
specs.generation_recipe: Label common_nouns.txt in chunks of 100 as living / nonliving / ambiguous. Living = names an organism (animal, plant, person, occupation/role). EXCLUDE (mark ambiguous): body parts ('heart', 'leaf' as detached part), dead-organism products ('leather', 'wood', 'meat'), collectives ('forest', 'crowd'), abstract nouns, and microorganism/borderline items ('virus'). Self-check: independent second labeling pass; keep only items where both passes agree and neither says ambiguous. Balance classes to at most 60/40.

specs.name: natural_manmade
specs.rule: Classify a concrete noun as naturally occurring (natural) or made by humans (manmade).
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), filtered by LLM to unambiguous cases
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — fixed binary label set; artifact-vs-natural-kind is a robust lexical semantic axis
specs.generation_recipe: Label common_nouns.txt in chunks as natural / manmade / ambiguous. EXCLUDE (ambiguous): cultivated or processed borderline items ('garden', 'farm', 'bread', 'paper', 'pearl'), domesticated animals if the labeler hesitates (default: animals and plants are natural), abstract nouns, and places mixing both ('park', 'harbor'). Self-check: two independent labeling passes; keep only double-agreement items with no ambiguous vote.

specs.name: concrete_abstract
specs.rule: Classify a noun as concrete (a physical thing you can see or touch) or abstract (an idea, quality, or state).
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), filtered by LLM to clear extremes; optionally cross-checked against published concreteness norms behavior via wordfreq availability
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — binary semantic judgment; concreteness is well represented in distributional statistics
specs.generation_recipe: Label common_nouns.txt in chunks as concrete / abstract / middle, instructing the labeler to use 'middle' liberally. KEEP only clear extremes: physical objects/substances/animals vs qualities/emotions/concepts. EXCLUDE (middle): events ('party', 'war'), time periods, sounds/light ('noise', 'shadow'), institutions ('school' building-vs-institution polysemy), and any noun with a common concrete AND abstract sense ('key', 'field'). Self-check: two independent passes; retain double-agreed extremes only; balance classes ~50/50.

specs.name: animal_plant_object
specs.rule: Classify a concrete noun as animal, plant, or object.
specs.domain_source: LLM-enumerated animals (~600) and plants/trees/flowers (~350) plus inanimate concrete nouns from common_nouns.txt (~600)
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news — small fixed label set over highly familiar items; basic taxonomic category is the easiest semantic feature
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate animals in chunks (mammals, birds, fish, insects, reptiles) and plants in chunks (trees, flowers, vegetables-as-plants, herbs, shrubs); take object-class items from common_nouns.txt concrete artifacts. EXCLUDE: plant products that read as food/objects ('apple' fruit-vs-tree, 'wood', 'cotton'), animal products ('wool', 'leather'), fungi and microorganisms, people/occupations. Self-check: independent 3-way relabeling pass; keep agreements; verify rare species names exist via an existence pass.

specs.name: person_place_thing
specs.rule: Classify a noun as person (a human or human role), place (a location), or thing (a physical object).
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000): occupations/roles (~500), location nouns (~400), object nouns (~1500)
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news — fixed 3-way label set; person/place/thing is a grade-school-salient distinction with massive corpus support
specs.generation_recipe: Label common_nouns.txt in chunks as person / place / thing / other-or-ambiguous. person = humans and roles ('teacher', 'uncle'); place = locations one can be at ('beach', 'kitchen', 'stadium'); thing = touchable objects. EXCLUDE ('other'): abstract nouns, events, animals, institutions with building/organization polysemy ('church', 'school', 'bank'), vehicles used as places ('ship' — drop). Self-check: two independent passes; keep double-agreements only; balance classes to within 2:1.

specs.name: animal_class
specs.rule: Given an animal, output its taxonomic class from the fixed set {mammal, bird, fish, reptile, insect}.
specs.domain_source: LLM-enumerated animal names including species, breeds, and common names: mammals ~450 (incl. dog/cat/horse breeds), birds ~300, fish ~250, reptiles ~120, insects ~180
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news / person-sport — fixed-label classification requiring item-level knowledge; grade-school biology but with a long tail of species names, hence medium
specs.generation_recipe: Enumerate per class in chunks, using breeds (dog, cat, horse, chicken... wait chicken is bird breeds fine) and species common names to reach counts. EXCLUDE: amphibians and arachnids entirely (not in label set — no frogs, spiders, scorpions), colloquial misleads ('jellyfish', 'starfish', 'silverfish' — not fish; 'bat' KEEP as mammal since it is crisp knowledge), extinct animals, and any name the existence-check pass cannot confirm. Self-check: independent blind classification pass over the 5 labels; keep agreements; run a third existence/commonness pass on the rare tail and drop uncertain species.

specs.name: singular_or_plural
specs.rule: Given a noun form, output singular or plural.
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000): each noun contributes its singular form and its lemminflect plural, minus exclusions
specs.difficulty_anchor: singular-plural — same morphological knowledge, recast as classification; surface -s cue makes it very learnable
specs.generation_recipe: For each noun in common_nouns.txt: emit (lemma, 'singular') and (lemminflect NNS inflection, 'plural'). EXCLUDE: invariant plurals ('sheep', 'series' — drop any noun whose plural equals its singular), uncountable/mass nouns (no natural plural: drop if lemminflect plural is rarely attested, wordfreq zipf(plural) < 2.5), pluralia tantum ('scissors', 'pants' — drop nouns whose singular form is rarer than the plural), and words ending in -s in the singular ('bus' KEEP but verify plural differs; 'lens' fine). Deterministic; self-check by asserting singular != plural for every emitted pair and sampling 200 for an LLM sanity pass.

specs.name: countable_uncountable
specs.rule: Given an English noun, output countable if it takes a plural and numerals naturally, or uncountable if it is a mass noun.
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), labeled by LLM with lemminflect/wordfreq plural-attestation as a mechanical prefilter
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — binary grammatical judgment; count/mass is strongly cued by distributional patterns ('much X' vs 'many Xs') a 6B model has seen constantly
specs.generation_recipe: Prefilter common_nouns.txt: candidate uncountables = nouns whose lemminflect plural has wordfreq zipf < 2.5 or is unattested; candidate countables = nouns with zipf(plural) >= 3.5. Then LLM-label each candidate countable/uncountable/both in chunks. EXCLUDE ('both'): nouns with common count and mass senses ('coffee', 'paper', 'hair', 'glass', 'chicken', 'experience'). Keep clear cases only ('advice', 'luggage', 'courage' vs 'chair', 'dog', 'window'). Self-check: two independent labeling passes; keep double-agreements; cap countables at ~60% of the set (uncountables are the scarce class, expect ~400-600 — if under 1200 total, relax the countable cap since countables are abundant).

specs.name: verb_to_gerund
specs.rule: Given a verb in base form, output its gerund/present-participle (-ing) form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt (3610) + lemminflect getInflection(v,'VBG')
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: identical single-step verb inflection, just a different target form; GPT-J does present-past well
specs.generation_recipe: For each alphabetic verb v in common_verbs.txt, g = lemminflect.getInflection(v,'VBG'). Keep pair (v, g[0]) if g is non-empty, len(g)==1 (drop multi-form outputs), and g[0]!=v. Deduplicate inputs. Verified domain: 3608 pairs.

specs.name: verb_to_third_person
specs.rule: Given a verb in base form, output its third-person singular present (-s) form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt (3610) + lemminflect getInflection(v,'VBZ')
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: same single-step inflection pattern with a different suffix; regular and common
specs.generation_recipe: For each alphabetic verb v in common_verbs.txt, f = lemminflect.getInflection(v,'VBZ'). Keep (v, f[0]) if len(f)==1 and f[0]!=v (excludes modals like 'can','may' which lemminflect handles as no-change or missing; explicitly drop 'be','have' style multi-form outputs). Deduplicate inputs. Verified domain: 3607.

specs.name: past_to_base
specs.rule: Given a verb in past tense, output its base (infinitive) form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt inverted through lemminflect getInflection(v,'VBD')
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past run in reverse: same lexical knowledge, inverse direction; lemmatization is a very common pattern in pretraining data
specs.generation_recipe: Build dict past_form -> set(base verbs) over all alphabetic v in common_verbs.txt using getInflection(v,'VBD')[0]. Keep only past forms that (a) map to exactly one base verb, (b) differ from the base ('put'-type zero-change excluded), (c) are single-form (drop 'was/were'). Input = past form, output = base. Verified domain: 3565 unique past forms.

specs.name: gerund_to_base
specs.rule: Given a verb's -ing form, output its base (infinitive) form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt inverted through lemminflect getInflection(v,'VBG')
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: single-step de-inflection, highly regular orthographic rule (drop -ing, undo doubling/e-drop)
specs.generation_recipe: Build dict gerund -> set(base verbs) over common_verbs.txt via getInflection(v,'VBG')[0]. Keep gerunds mapping to exactly one base verb; input = gerund, output = base. Verified domain: 3598 unique gerunds.

specs.name: third_person_to_base
specs.rule: Given a verb's third-person singular present (-s) form, output its base form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt inverted through lemminflect getInflection(v,'VBZ')
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: same class of one-step de-inflection; -s stripping is trivial surface morphology
specs.generation_recipe: Build dict vbz_form -> set(base verbs) over common_verbs.txt via getInflection(v,'VBZ')[0]. Keep forms with exactly one source verb and form != base. Note the noun-plural homograph (e.g. 'walks' as noun) does not create ambiguity because the output is the same string either way. Estimated domain ~3500 after uniqueness filter.

specs.name: past_to_gerund
specs.rule: Given a verb in past tense, output the same verb's -ing form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt via lemminflect: VBD form -> VBG form of same lemma
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: same lexical material but form-to-form conversion (implicitly via the lemma); slightly harder than base-form inflection, hence medium
specs.generation_recipe: For each verb v in common_verbs.txt compute p=getInflection(v,'VBD')[0], g=getInflection(v,'VBG')[0]. Keep (p,g) if p maps to exactly one lemma (reuse past_to_base uniqueness set), p!=v, and both are single-form. Input = past, output = gerund. Domain: 3565 unique pasts.

specs.name: gerund_to_past
specs.rule: Given a verb's -ing form, output the same verb's past tense.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt via lemminflect: VBG form -> VBD form of same lemma
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: identical output space (past forms) but from an inflected input; one implicit lemmatize step, hence medium
specs.generation_recipe: For each verb v in common_verbs.txt compute g=getInflection(v,'VBG')[0], p=getInflection(v,'VBD')[0]. Keep (g,p) if g maps to exactly one lemma and p is single-form and p!=v is not required (output may equal lemma for irregulars like 'put' -> keep, still deterministic). Domain: 3598 unique gerunds.

specs.name: gerund_to_third_person
specs.rule: Given a verb's -ing form, output the same verb's third-person singular present (-s) form.
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt via lemminflect: VBG form -> VBZ form of same lemma
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: form-to-form conversion between two regular inflections; near-orthographic (-ing -> -s), hence medium-plus
specs.generation_recipe: For each verb v in common_verbs.txt compute g=getInflection(v,'VBG')[0], s=getInflection(v,'VBZ')[0]. Keep (g,s) if g maps to exactly one lemma and s is single-form and s!=g. Domain: 3598 unique gerunds.

specs.name: plural_to_singular
specs.rule: Given a plural noun, output its singular form.
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000) inverted through lemminflect getInflection(n,'NNS')
specs.difficulty_anchor: singular-plural run in reverse; same knowledge, inverse mapping (repo already pairs next/prev tasks this way)
specs.generation_recipe: Build dict plural -> set(singulars) over alphabetic nouns in common_nouns.txt via getInflection(n,'NNS')[0]. Keep plurals that map to exactly one singular and differ from it (drops invariants like 'sheep','series'). Input = plural, output = singular. Verified domain: 5369.

specs.name: noun_possessive
specs.rule: Given a singular noun, output its possessive form (noun + 's).
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), pure string rule
specs.difficulty_anchor: singular-plural: appending a clitic to a noun, same operation class and regularity
specs.generation_recipe: For each alphabetic noun n in common_nouns.txt that does not end in 's' (avoids the s'/s's style variation), output n + "'s". No other edge cases. Domain: ~5500 of 6000 nouns.

specs.name: adjective_to_adverb
specs.rule: Given an adjective, output the corresponding -ly adverb.
specs.domain_source: common_adjs.txt + adjectives from wordfreq top_n_list('en',100000) filtered by lemminflect getAllLemmas ADJ; derived adverb validated with wordfreq
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past: single regular suffixation with small orthographic adjustments; -ly derivation is at least as frequent in text
specs.generation_recipe: Adjective pool = common_adjs.txt plus alphabetic words in wordfreq top 100k whose getAllLemmas contains ADJ; exclude words already ending in -ly. Derive adverb: consonant+'le' -> replace final 'e' with 'y' (gentle->gently); consonant+'y' -> -ily (happy->happily); -ic -> -ically (basic->basically); else +ly. Keep pair only if zipf_frequency(adverb)>=2.0 (validates the derived form exists). Exclude irregulars by construction (good->goodly is filtered only by frequency, so additionally hard-exclude {good, fast, hard, late, early}). Verified domain: 1410.

specs.name: adverb_to_adjective
specs.rule: Given an -ly adverb, output the adjective it is derived from.
specs.domain_source: inverse of adjective_to_adverb pair list (same pools and wordfreq validation)
specs.difficulty_anchor: singular-plural reverse-direction analogy: undoing one regular suffix; surface-decodable from the input string
specs.generation_recipe: Take the validated (adjective, adverb) pairs from the adjective_to_adverb recipe and invert them. Keep only adverbs that map to exactly one adjective under the inverse orthographic rules (drop collisions). Input = adverb, output = adjective. Domain ~1400.

specs.name: agent_noun
specs.rule: Given a verb, output the agent noun formed with -er/-or (the person or thing that does the action).
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt + verbs from wordfreq top 100k (getAllLemmas VERB, lemma==surface); candidate -er/-or forms validated with wordfreq
specs.difficulty_anchor: present-past plus a touch of lexical lookup (er vs or); agentive derivation is extremely frequent in pretraining text
specs.generation_recipe: Verb pool = common_verbs.txt plus alphabetic wordfreq-top-100k words whose getAllLemmas VERB lemma equals the surface form. Candidates per verb: v+'er' and v+'or'; if v ends in 'e': v+'r' and v[:-1]+'or'; consonant+'y': v[:-1]+'ier'; monosyllabic CVC: doubled consonant +'er'. Keep the verb iff exactly ONE candidate has zipf_frequency>=2.2 (uniqueness makes the mapping deterministic and drops er/or ambiguity like 'convert'). Verified domain: 1233. Self-check: sample 100 pairs, confirm the output is an attested English noun via wordfreq zipf>=2.2 and manual spot-check for semantic agentivity (drop instrumentals that look wrong, e.g. 'timer' is fine, keep).

specs.name: agent_noun_to_verb
specs.rule: Given an -er/-or agent noun, output the verb it is derived from.
specs.domain_source: inverse of agent_noun pair list
specs.difficulty_anchor: past_to_base analogy: undoing one derivational suffix, surface-decodable; slightly easier than the forward direction
specs.generation_recipe: Invert the validated (verb, agent) pairs from the agent_noun recipe; keep agents that map to exactly one verb. Input = agent noun, output = verb. Domain: 1233.

specs.name: strip_prefix
specs.rule: Given a word formed with a derivational prefix (un-, re-, dis-, mis-, non-, over-, under-, pre-), output the base word with the prefix removed.
specs.domain_source: wordfreq top 100k scanned for prefix+base where base is in common_words.txt; LLM opacity filter
specs.difficulty_anchor: antonym (which contains many un- pairs) crossed with a simple surface deletion; the string cue makes it easier than pure antonym
specs.generation_recipe: Scan alphabetic words w (len>=5, zipf>=2.3) in wordfreq top 100k. For prefixes [un,re,dis,mis,non,over,under,pre]: if w startswith prefix, base=w[len(p):], keep if len(base)>=3, base in common_words.txt, zipf(base)>=3.0. Exclude words matching more than one prefix split. Then LLM-filter opaque splits where the word is NOT semantically prefix+base (e.g. 'restrain'!='re'+'strain', 'discover', 'preside', 'republic') — batch-ask an LLM 'is X literally PREFIX + BASE in meaning? yes/no' and drop 'no'. Measured 972 pairs at stricter thresholds before relaxation, so >=1300 after threshold relaxation and before opacity filtering; verify final count >=1200, else add prefixes [anti, sub, co, out]. Self-check: 50-pair manual audit for opacity leakage.

specs.name: pos_label
specs.rule: Given a word with only one part of speech, output that part of speech (noun, verb, adjective, or adverb).
specs.domain_source: common_words.txt filtered to single-POS words via lemminflect getAllLemmas
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment / ag_news: closed small label set over a lexical input; POS is shallower knowledge than news topic
specs.generation_recipe: For each alphabetic word in common_words.txt, compute getAllLemmas(w) restricted to {NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV}; keep words with exactly one POS key. Map to labels 'noun'/'verb'/'adjective'/'adverb'. Verified domain: 6603 (3483 noun, 1558 verb, 1126 adj, 436 adv). Balance classes when sampling prompts. Self-check: spot-check 50 words against wordfreq usage; drop any that an LLM flags as commonly used in a second POS (lemminflect misses some conversions).

specs.name: verb_tense_label
specs.rule: Given an inflected verb form, output which inflection it is: past, gerund, or present (third-person -s).
specs.domain_source: common_verbs.txt inflected via lemminflect VBD/VBG/VBZ, collision-filtered
specs.difficulty_anchor: ag_news: 3-way closed-label classification; the -ed/-ing/-s suffix cue is strongly surface-visible
specs.generation_recipe: For each verb in common_verbs.txt generate (VBD,'past'), (VBG,'gerund'), (VBZ,'present') forms. Build form->set(labels) across all verbs and keep only forms with exactly one label (drops collisions like 'put' base=past). Verified domain: 10777 (3571 past, 3601 gerund, 3605 present). Balance labels when sampling prompts.

specs.name: article_choice
specs.rule: Given a singular noun, output the correct indefinite article, 'a' or 'an', determined by the noun's initial sound.
specs.domain_source: common_nouns.txt (6000), letter rule + explicit exception lists
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter: a property of the word onset; a/an choice is among the most reinforced patterns in English text
specs.generation_recipe: For each alphabetic noun in common_nouns.txt: default label 'an' if first letter in aeiou else 'a'. Override list A (vowel letter but consonant sound -> 'a'): words starting with 'uni','use','user','usu','ute','uto','ura','eu', plus {one, once, ewe, ukulele, ubiquity}. Override list B (silent h -> 'an'): words starting with 'hour','honest','honor','honour','heir'. Any word matching neither a clean default nor an explicit override pattern but starting with 'u','eu','h' gets checked by LLM once and added to the appropriate list; ambiguous pronunciations (e.g. 'herb' US/UK) are excluded. Domain ~6000.

specs.name: word_polarity
specs.rule: Given a strongly evaluative English word, output whether its connotation is positive or negative.
specs.domain_source: NLTK opinion_lexicon (Bing Liu, 2006 positive / 4783 negative words) intersected with wordfreq zipf>=2.5; LLM fallback if corpus unavailable
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment: same label space, but word-level polarity of strongly polar words is easier than review-level sentiment
specs.generation_recipe: Primary: nltk.corpus.opinion_lexicon positive()/negative() lists; keep alphabetic words with zipf_frequency>=2.5; drop words appearing in both lists or in common ironic/ambiguous set (e.g. 'killer','sick','cheap' -> LLM double-check any word an LLM rates below 90% confident). Fallback if NLTK download unavailable: LLM-generate 800 clearly positive and 800 clearly negative common words in batches, deduplicate, keep only words the LLM labels identically across 3 independent prompts, filter zipf>=2.5. Self-check: relabel a 200-word sample with a differently-worded prompt; require 98% agreement, drop disagreements.

specs.name: hypernym_category
specs.rule: Given a common noun, output its superordinate category from a fixed set of 18 labels (beverage, bird, building, clothing, fabric, fish, flower, fruit, furniture, instrument, metal, profession, sport, tool, tree, vegetable, vehicle, weapon).
specs.domain_source: WordNet hyponym closures of the 12 category synsets, intersected with wordfreq zipf>=2.7; LLM verification pass
specs.difficulty_anchor: person-occupation: entity -> category-label lookup with a small label set; 'X is a kind of Y' is classic distributional knowledge GPT-J handles
specs.generation_recipe: For each of 12 category synsets (bird.n.01, fish.n.01, tree.n.01, flower.n.01, edible_fruit.n.01, vegetable.n.01, tool.n.01, clothing.n.01, furniture.n.01, vehicle.n.01, musical_instrument.n.01, metallic_element.n.01) collect single-word lemma hyponyms with zipf>=2.7. Exclusions: words in more than one closure; polysemous words whose most frequent sense is outside the category (LLM check: 'what is a(n) X primarily? one word'); NO animal-class labels beyond bird/fish (keeps it disjoint from the separate animal_class task); metals capped by nature (~30) — the bulk comes from the other 11. Verify total >=1200 after filtering; if short, add categories (fabric, beverage, weapon). Self-check: LLM relabels 200-item sample against the fixed label set, require 97% agreement.

specs.name: compound_head
specs.rule: Given a closed compound noun, output its head — the final constituent word.
specs.domain_source: LLM-curated list of genuine English closed compounds, orthographically verified against common_words.txt and wordfreq
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_last_letter: extract a determined part of the input word, but the split point is lexical rather than positional; compounds are transparent to GPT-J's tokenizer-adjacent knowledge
specs.generation_recipe: LLM-generate candidate closed compounds in themed batches (household, nature, body, transport, sports, food, weather, work...) targeting 2000 candidates. Programmatic verification: compound is alphabetic, zipf>=2.0, and equals part1+part2 where both parts are in common_words.txt with zipf>=3.3 and len>=3. Exclusions: words with more than one valid two-word split into common words where an LLM judges both splits plausible (drop); pseudo-compounds that pass string checks but are not compositional ('history','person','rather' — the LLM curation step, not string scanning, is the primary source precisely to avoid these); second parts in the suffix-like set {ing, er, ed, ion, ness, ment, able, age}. A raw string scan of wordfreq top-50k yields 2484 candidate splits, so after curation >=1500 genuine compounds is realistic; verify >=1200. Self-check: 100-item manual audit that part2 is truly the semantic head.

specs.name: compound_first
specs.rule: Given a closed compound noun, output its first constituent word (the modifier).
specs.domain_source: same curated compound list as compound_head
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize_first_letter analogy of compound_head: same lexical segmentation, other constituent; equal difficulty
specs.generation_recipe: Reuse the verified (compound, part1, part2) triples from the compound_head recipe; output part1. Same exclusions apply (unique split required). Domain identical, ~1500.

specs.name: compound_join
specs.rule: Given two words that form a standard closed compound, output the compound written as one word.
specs.domain_source: same curated compound list, inverted (two-word input)
specs.difficulty_anchor: capitalize: near-copy orthographic transform (concatenate two given words); lexical validation is implicit, so easier than the split direction
specs.generation_recipe: Reuse verified triples from compound_head; input = 'part1 part2' (space-separated, 2 words <= 4-word limit), output = compound. Keep only pairs whose concatenation is the attested compound (already guaranteed). Domain ~1500.

specs.name: larger_than_1000
specs.rule: Given an integer other than 1000, output 'yes' if it is greater than 1000, otherwise 'no'.
specs.domain_source: pure rule: integers 1-99 union 101-99999, balanced 50/50 across the threshold
specs.difficulty_anchor: sentiment — binary classification; the threshold check is equivalent to 'has 3+ digits', which is a length judgment like word_length
specs.generation_recipe: 500 seeded ints in [2,999] ('no') + 500 in [1001,50000] ('yes'), shuffled seed 42.

specs.name: number_word_to_digits
specs.rule: Given a number spelled out in English words (21-1500), output it in digits.
specs.domain_source: rule (numbers 21-1500)
specs.difficulty_anchor: next_number_digits / ordinal_suffix: number-format conversion, short digit outputs
specs.generation_recipe: see repairs_round1.py spell()

specs.name: last_vowel
specs.rule: Word -> the last vowel (a,e,i,o,u) reading right to left.
specs.domain_source: common_words.txt
specs.difficulty_anchor: first_vowel: mirrored scan direction
specs.generation_recipe: see repairs_round1.py
